source.title: The validity and utility of selection methods in personnel psychology: Practical and theoretical implications of 85 years of research findings
source.author: Frank L. Schmidt and John E. Hunter

ideas.title: Never use a camp stove, grill or heater inside a tent
ideas.body: The CDC warns that burning fuel in a tent or camper produces carbon monoxide, which can kill in a sleeping space. Cook outside, never bring a grill or gas heater inside, and use a battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm in an RV.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless and blocks oxygen in the blood. Small enclosed spaces fill quickly. Sleep makes it harder to notice symptoms like headache and dizziness.

Example: On a cold night, campers consider bringing a charcoal grill into the tent for warmth. One recalls the warning and instead adds layers and a warm sleeping bag.

Apply it today: Add a battery CO alarm to your camper kit. If anyone feels dizzy or sick, get everyone outside and call emergency services. Take a hands-on wilderness first aid course.

source.title: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Camping (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)

ideas.title: You can look straight at something and not see it
ideas.body: In the 'invisible gorilla' study, viewers counting basketball passes often failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. About half missed it.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Attention is selective, and when it is tied up on one task, unexpected things go unseen. This is inattentional blindness. Confidence that you would notice is itself misplaced.

Example: A driver focused on a phone call does not register a cyclist in clear view. Looking is not the same as seeing.

Apply it today: When doing something critical, such as driving, remove other demands on your attention. Before starting, ask yourself what you might be missing.

source.title: Gorillas in our midst: Sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events
source.author: Daniel J. Simons and Christopher F. Chabris

ideas.title: The Mongols built a relay network to move messages and merchants
ideas.body: The Mongol Empire ran a relay system called the Yam. Stations along main routes held fresh horses, food and lodging, so riders carrying messages could swap mounts and keep moving. Officials traveled on it with a metal tablet as authority.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Empires are held together by information speed. A relay avoids the limit of one tired rider or horse, because the message moves while the animals rest. Stations also needed supplies from local people, which made the burden political.

Example: The network let the rulers send orders across a vast territory and also helped trade and travelers, so protection of roads was a source of wealth. The same relay logic is used in modern networks that pass data along nodes.

Apply it today: Think of a task you do alone from start to finish and break it into stages handed off to others. Find one you could pass on.

source.title: Yam (route)

ideas.title: Feeling like a fraud is common among people who succeed
ideas.body: Many capable people believe their success is luck and fear being exposed. Psychologists call this the impostor phenomenon. It is a pattern of thinking, not a medical diagnosis, and it is widespread among high achievers.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes first described it in 1978, in a group of high-achieving women. The core trap is that praise is discounted and mistakes are magnified, so evidence of competence never sticks.

Example: After a promotion you think 'they will find out'. You write a list of five things you delivered and the feedback you got, and share your worry with a mentor, who says they felt the same way early on.

Apply it today: Write down three concrete results from the past year with a name or number each. Read the list before your next big task, and tell one trusted person how you feel.

source.title: The impostor phenomenon in high achieving women: Dynamics and therapeutic intervention
source.author: Pauline Rose Clance and Suzanne Ament Imes

ideas.title: Anchor TVs and heavy furniture so they cannot tip onto a child
ideas.body: The Consumer Product Safety Commission warns that furniture and TV tip-overs injure and kill children. Anchor dressers, bookcases and TVs to the wall with straps or brackets, and put heavy items on low shelves.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Children climb, and a few pounds of pull can topple a dresser. Anchors hold it in place. The CPSC's Anchor It campaign provides guidance.

Example: A family buys a tall dresser and uses wall brackets. Later, a toddler pulls the top drawer open and climbs, and the dresser stays upright.

Apply it today: Anchor one piece of furniture this weekend. If a piece falls on someone, call emergency services and lift it off. Take a child first aid class for hands-on practice.

source.title: Anchor It (U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission)

ideas.title: Believing a treatment will help can change how you feel
ideas.body: The placebo effect: inert treatments can relieve some symptoms, especially pain and nausea, because of expectation and context. It works on how symptoms are experienced, not on underlying disease.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Expectation and the ritual of care alter perception and brain activity. This is why trials compare treatments with placebos. It also shows why a caring manner and clear explanation can improve how patients feel.

Example: In a trial, a sugar pill given with confidence eases pain for some participants. They were not faking. The brain really changed the experience.

Apply it today: When you start a helpful habit, set a realistic expectation of benefit. Do not use placebo belief as a reason to skip proven medical care.

source.title: Placebo

ideas.title: A league of merchant towns ran northern trade with no state behind it
ideas.body: From the thirteenth century, merchants of northern German towns such as Lubeck formed the Hanseatic League. They traded timber, fur, grain and fish across the Baltic and North Sea. It was an alliance of towns, not a country, built for protection and shared rules.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Trade over distance needs trust: contracts, safe harbors, and a way to punish cheats. The league provided common rules, trading posts abroad and collective bargaining. Members could refuse to trade with a place that wronged one of them, a strong lever.

Example: Cities such as Bergen and London hosted league outposts. Over time, powerful nation states and shifting trade routes weakened it. It shows that institutions can create trust at scale without a central government.

Apply it today: Think of a group where trust is low, such as a shared flat or team. Write one clear rule everyone follows, and see how it changes behavior.

source.title: Hanseatic League

ideas.title: A walk can lift your creative output while you are moving
ideas.body: In experiments at Stanford, Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz asked people to come up with new uses for everyday objects. Participants generated more creative answers while walking than while sitting, and the boost carried over for a short time afterward.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Light movement seems to loosen free-flowing thinking, though it does not help every kind of problem. The study found gains for open-ended idea generation and less benefit for tasks with a single correct answer. It was a small experimental study, so treat the size of the effect with caution.

Example: Instead of staring at a blank page, you take a ten minute loop and talk through three possible angles for the project, then write them down when you return.

Apply it today: The next time you need ideas rather than answers, walk for ten minutes before you sit down, and note down what comes up as soon as you stop.

source.title: Give your ideas some legs: The positive effect of walking on creative thinking
source.author: Marily Oppezzo and Daniel L. Schwartz

ideas.title: Set your water heater to 120 degrees Fahrenheit to prevent scalds
ideas.body: The Consumer Product Safety Commission advises setting the water heater thermostat to 120 degrees Fahrenheit or lower. Hotter water can scald a child's skin in seconds. Test bath water with your wrist or elbow before use.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Skin burns faster at higher temperatures, and children's skin is thinner. A lower setting turns a serious burn risk into a mild one. It also saves energy.

Example: A landlord checks the thermostat and finds it set high. Lowering it to 120 and testing the tap protects the new baby in the flat.

Apply it today: Check your water temperature with a thermometer. For burns, cool under running water for 20 minutes and call for help if severe. Learn burn care in a hands-on Red Cross class.

source.title: Scald burn prevention (U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission)

ideas.title: People often put in less effort when working as a group
ideas.body: Social loafing: Latane, Williams and Harkins found that people shouted and clapped less loudly when they thought others were also doing so than when they knew they alone were being measured.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: When individual contribution is invisible, effort drops. Making each person's output identifiable and meaningful reduces this. Small groups and clear roles help.

Example: A group project with a shared grade ends with three people doing most of the work. Assigning each member a named section and reviewing it separately brings the effort back.

Apply it today: On your next team task, give each person a named piece and a date. Make the individual results visible to the group.

source.title: Many hands make light the work: The causes and consequences of social loafing
source.author: Bibb Latane, Kipling Williams and Stephen Harkins

ideas.title: Medieval bankers hid interest inside exchange rates
ideas.body: The Medici bank, based in Florence, grew in the fifteenth century by moving money across Europe with bills of exchange. A merchant could pay in one city and be paid in another, without carrying coins. Interest was built into the exchange rate, avoiding church bans on lending at interest.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: A bill of exchange is a written order to pay a sum in another place and currency. Safety from robbers was one benefit. The banker earned from the gap between rates in each city, which seemed to be a currency service rather than a loan.

Example: The Medici ran branches in cities such as Venice, Bruges and Rome, each as a partnership with a local manager. The bank declined in the late fifteenth century after bad loans to rulers. It shows how financial tools grow around legal gaps.

Apply it today: Look at a recent foreign payment or card fee, and find the exchange rate margin hidden in it. Compare it to the mid-market rate.

source.title: Medici Bank

ideas.title: Searching for the perfect job can make you happier with worse results
ideas.body: A study of graduating students found that those who tried to find the best job, called maximizers, got somewhat higher salaries but were less satisfied with their jobs and felt more stress and regret than those who looked for a good enough one.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Sheena Iyengar, Rachael Wells and Barry Schwartz found that comparing many options raises expectations and doubt. Satisficers, who pick the first option that meets their criteria, usually end up happier even when the offer is slightly worse.

Example: You apply to 40 roles and keep re-ranking them, worried you missed a better one. A friend lists four must-haves, takes the first offer that meets them and starts working happily.

Apply it today: Write down three must-have criteria for your next big choice, whether a job, flat or purchase. Pick the first option that meets them and stop searching.

source.title: Doing Better but Feeling Worse: Looking for the 'Best' Job Undermines Satisfaction
source.author: Sheena S. Iyengar, Rachael E. Wells and Barry Schwartz

ideas.title: Treat every downed power line as live and stay far away
ideas.body: After storms, fallen lines may still carry deadly current, even when they look dead or do not spark. Stay far back, keep others away, and call the utility and emergency services. Do not touch anything in contact with the line.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Electricity travels through the ground and objects like wet branches or fences. You cannot tell by looking whether a wire is energized. Distance and a call are the only safe actions.

Example: After a windstorm, a wire lies across a neighbor's lawn. Instead of moving it with a stick, a resident calls 911 and warns children to stay back until the crew arrives.

Apply it today: Save your utility's emergency number in your phone. Never drive over a downed line. Join a local CERT course for hands-on storm response training.

source.title: Power Outages (Ready.gov, FEMA)

ideas.title: Procrastination is about managing mood, not managing time
ideas.body: Sirois and Pychyl argue that procrastinators put off tasks to escape bad feelings, like boredom or anxiety, in the short term, at the cost of the future self.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Avoiding the task brings immediate relief, which reinforces the habit. The better target is the feeling the task triggers, not the calendar. Making the first step small and less threatening reduces the pull to escape.

Example: You avoid writing a hard email because you dread the reply. You tidy your desk instead and feel better for a minute. The dread stays.

Apply it today: Name the feeling the task brings up. Then commit to five minutes on the least scary part, and stop after that if you want.

source.title: Procrastination and the priority of short-term mood regulation: Consequences for future self
source.author: Fuschia M. Sirois and Timothy A. Pychyl

ideas.title: Haiti had to pay France for its freedom for over a century
ideas.body: In 1825, after Haiti won independence, France demanded payment for lost property in return for recognition, with warships nearby. Haiti borrowed from French banks to pay, and the debts were not fully cleared until 1947. Economists link this burden to lasting weakness.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: The payments drained the young state's revenue, and the loans added interest and fees. Money that could have built schools and roads went abroad. Debt imposed at independence set a trap that lasted generations.

Example: The sum was later reduced, but remained heavy. Haiti was the first country founded by formerly enslaved people, and the major powers were hostile to it. The case is used in debates about how past events shape present wealth.

Apply it today: Pick one country's current economic problem and search for its history of debt or sanctions. See whether a link from the past is documented.

source.title: Haitian indemnity controversy

ideas.title: Mentally switching off after work helps you do better tomorrow
ideas.body: In a diary study, employees who psychologically detached from work in the evening, not thinking about tasks or checking messages, felt more engaged at work the next day.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Sabine Sonnentag studied how recovery during off-hours shapes next-day behaviour. Detaching lets the mental resources used at work refill. Continuing to ruminate about work keeps you in effort mode and leaves you drained.

Example: A manager closes her laptop at 6, takes a walk, cooks and avoids email until the morning. Colleagues notice she arrives sharper than the one who replies to messages at 10 pm.

Apply it today: Pick a shutdown ritual tonight, such as writing tomorrow's top three tasks, closing the laptop and silencing work notifications until morning.

source.title: Recovery, work engagement, and proactive behavior: A new look at the interface between nonwork and work
source.author: Sabine Sonnentag

ideas.title: Strength and balance exercise lowers the risk of a serious fall
ideas.body: The CDC's STEADI program for fall prevention suggests older adults do exercises that improve strength and balance, review medicines that cause dizziness, check vision, and remove home hazards like loose rugs. A fall is often the start of lasting harm.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Falls are a leading cause of injury in older adults, and the causes stack up: weak legs, poor balance, medicine side effects, and hazards. Fixing several together works better than one.

Example: A grandmother joins a tai chi class, replaces a frayed rug, and asks her pharmacist to review her pills. Over the year she feels steadier.

Apply it today: Remove one trip hazard today and ask a clinician about balance exercises. If someone falls and cannot get up or hits their head, call emergency services. Take a hands-on first aid class.

source.title: STEADI: Older Adult Fall Prevention (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)

ideas.title: Walking can lift your creative output
ideas.body: Oppezzo and Schwartz found that people generated more creative ideas while walking than sitting, and the boost lingered for a short while after they sat back down.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Gentle movement may loosen up thinking and help free-flowing idea generation. It helped with divergent thinking, which is coming up with many ideas, rather than with problems that have one right answer.

Example: Stuck on a title for your talk, you take a ten-minute walk and return with several options.

Apply it today: Next time you need ideas, take a walk, indoors or out, and bring a notepad or voice memo.

source.title: Give your ideas some legs: The positive effect of walking on creative thinking
source.author: Marily Oppezzo and Daniel L. Schwartz

ideas.title: Ice ages are paced by slow wobbles in Earth's orbit
ideas.body: Milankovitch cycles are regular changes in Earth's orbit shape, axis tilt and the direction the axis points. They shift how sunlight is spread across the seasons and latitudes over tens of thousands of years. A 1976 study of ocean sediments linked them to the pace of ice ages.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Small changes in summer sunlight at high northern latitudes decide whether snow melts. When it does not, ice builds and reflects more light, which cools further. The orbit sets the timing, while feedbacks make the response large.

Example: Researchers Hays, Imbrie and Shackleton found the cycles in oxygen isotope records from seabed cores. The tilt cycle is about 41,000 years. These cycles are far too slow to explain current warming, which is happening in decades.

Apply it today: Next time someone says climate has always changed, ask what drove each past change and how fast it happened. Compare rates, not just direction.

source.title: Variations in the Earth's Orbit: Pacemaker of the Ice Ages
source.author: J. D. Hays, John Imbrie and N. J. Shackleton

ideas.title: Check email in a few batches a day to feel less stressed
ideas.body: In an experiment, people who checked email only three times a day reported lower stress than those who checked as often as they liked. Fewer checks meant fewer interruptions without hurting their work.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Kostadin Kushlev and Elizabeth Dunn found that constant email checking raised daily stress, and that limiting it lowered it. Batching also reduces the cost of switching tasks that comes with each new message.

Example: You check email at 9, 1 and 4 and close the tab between. When something urgent arises, people can call you. By the end of the week you have spent hours on focused work.

Apply it today: Pick three set times to check email tomorrow, and close your email window outside them. Tell coworkers how to reach you for anything urgent.

source.title: Checking email less frequently reduces stress
source.author: Kostadin Kushlev and Elizabeth W. Dunn

ideas.title: On a ladder, keep three points of contact and set it at a 4 to 1 angle
ideas.body: NIOSH advises ladders be placed so the base is one foot away from the wall for every four feet of height. Keep three points of contact, two hands and one foot or two feet and one hand, and do not carry heavy loads while climbing.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: At the right angle, a ladder is stable without tipping back or sliding out. Three points of contact keeps your center of gravity over the rungs. Ladder falls cause many serious injuries.

Example: A homeowner cleans gutters. He sets the ladder at the right angle, hauls tools up on a rope, and keeps his belt buckle between the rails. Nothing goes wrong.

Apply it today: Check your ladder's rating and condition before the next job. Call emergency services after a serious fall and do not move the person. Take a hands-on work safety course.

source.title: Ladder Safety (National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health)

ideas.title: Be a fox, not a hedgehog, when you predict
ideas.body: Philip Tetlock studied expert predictions for years. Experts with one big theory, which he called hedgehogs, forecast worse than those who drew on many ideas and adjusted, the foxes.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: A single framework makes the world seem simple and tempts you to ignore evidence against it. Foxes combine perspectives, accept uncertainty and update. In his data, experts were often hardly better than chance on long-range political questions.

Example: A commentator with one big theory of markets predicts a crash every year. Another weighs several indicators and says 'maybe 30 percent'. The second is more useful and more often right.

Apply it today: Next time you predict something, write the strongest argument against your view and give your forecast as a percentage.

source.title: Expert Political Judgment: How Good Is It? How Can We Know?
source.author: Philip E. Tetlock

ideas.title: Tiny microbes once poisoned the air with oxygen and changed the planet
ideas.body: Around 2.4 billion years ago, bacteria that photosynthesize released oxygen faster than the Earth could absorb it. Oxygen then built up in the air, an event called the Great Oxidation. For many ancient microbes, oxygen was toxic.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: At first, oxygen reacted with iron in the oceans and rock, which formed layers of rust-colored minerals now seen as banded iron formations. Once that sink was full, the gas accumulated in the atmosphere. It opened the way for energy-rich life that breathes oxygen.

Example: The change was probably one of the largest mass extinctions of that era, though evidence is thin. Bands of red rock in places like Western Australia record it. Every breath you take depends on a change that began with single cells.

Apply it today: Look at a photo of a banded iron formation online and read its caption. Then take a slow breath and think of its source.

source.title: Great Oxidation Event

ideas.title: Small visible progress is the best driver of a good work day
ideas.body: Teresa Amabile and Steven Kramer studied thousands of work diary entries from hundreds of professionals. The days people felt most motivated were those on which they made progress in work that mattered to them, even small steps.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: They called this the progress principle. Progress gives a sense of meaning and competence, which feeds drive for the next step. Setbacks and blocked work do the reverse, so removing obstacles can matter as much as adding rewards.

Example: A writer finishes a single section of a long report and ticks it off a visible checklist. That small tick gives her the energy to start the next section after lunch.

Apply it today: Break one large task into five steps, write them down and tick off the first one before noon. At the end of the day, note one thing you moved forward.

source.title: The Progress Principle
source.author: Teresa Amabile and Steven Kramer

ideas.title: Check labels so you never take two products with acetaminophen
ideas.body: Acetaminophen, known as paracetamol, is in many cold, flu and pain products. The FDA warns that taking more than the labeled limit can cause liver damage. Read the Drug Facts label on each medicine and never combine two products with it.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Different products with different names can contain the same ingredient, so doses add up. Liver injury can be silent at first. Poison control can help if you are unsure.

Example: A man with flu takes a night cold remedy and then a pain tablet for his headache. Reading the labels, he sees both contain acetaminophen and skips the second.

Apply it today: Read the active ingredients on your medicine cabinet items. If you took too much, call poison control or emergency services at once. Ask a pharmacist, or take a first aid class for hands-on advice.

source.title: Acetaminophen: Safe Use (U.S. Food and Drug Administration)

ideas.title: Simple rules can beat complicated analysis
ideas.body: Gerd Gigerenzer and colleagues show that in uncertain situations, simple heuristics such as 'take the best clue' can match or beat complex models, because they ignore noise.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: With limited data, complex models overfit past noise and predict poorly. A rule with few inputs is more robust. The key is choosing the right simple rule for the environment.

Example: To pick a restaurant, you could compare dozens of reviews. Choosing the one where the locals eat is a single clue that often works well.

Apply it today: For your next small decision, pick the one criterion that matters most, decide on it, and stop researching.

source.title: Heuristic decision making
source.author: Gerd Gigerenzer and Wolfgang Gaissmaier

ideas.title: Remove one starfish and a whole shoreline changes
ideas.body: In the 1960s, ecologist Robert Paine removed the predatory starfish Pisaster from plots of Washington coast. Mussels spread, crowded out other species, and diversity fell sharply. His work gave us the idea of a keystone species.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: A keystone species has an outsized effect compared to its numbers. The starfish ate the mussels, which would otherwise dominate the space and light out competitors. Remove a predator and a food web can shift in ways hard to predict.

Example: Sea otters in kelp forests are another example: they eat urchins, which graze kelp. Where otters vanished, urchin numbers could rise and forests thin. The idea is a warning that not all species count equally in a system.

Apply it today: Walk through a local park and name one species you think holds the system together, then look up whether ecologists agree.

source.title: Food Web Complexity and Species Diversity
source.author: Robert T. Paine

ideas.title: People are far more willing to help than you expect
ideas.body: In experiments, people asked to request help from strangers expected far fewer yeses than they got. Asking feels risky to the asker, but the person asked often agrees, and may feel good about it.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Francis Flynn and Vanessa Lake found that we underestimate how awkward it is to refuse in person. That makes agreement more likely than we guess, so we avoid asking and lose out.

Example: A new employee struggles with a spreadsheet for two hours before asking a colleague, who fixes it in five minutes and says, 'Ask me anytime.'

Apply it today: Ask one person for help today on something you have been stuck on. Be specific, give a reason, and make it easy to say no.

source.title: If you need help, just ask: Underestimating compliance with direct requests for help
source.author: Francis J. Flynn and Vanessa K. B. Lake

ideas.title: Do not let someone 'sleep it off' if they may have alcohol poisoning
ideas.body: Signs of alcohol poisoning include confusion, vomiting, slow or irregular breathing, cold clammy or bluish skin, and passing out. Call emergency services, stay with the person, and turn them on their side so they do not choke.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Alcohol can keep rising in the blood after someone stops drinking, and it suppresses breathing and the gag reflex. Sleeping is not safe if they cannot be woken. Waiting can be deadly.

Example: At a party, a friend cannot be woken and is breathing slowly. Another guest calls 911, rolls him on his side, and stays until the ambulance arrives.

Apply it today: Memorise the signs and the rule: when in doubt, call. Learn the recovery position in a hands-on first aid class.

source.title: Alcohol Poisoning: Know the Facts (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)

ideas.title: A simple weighted checklist often judges as well as expert intuition
ideas.body: Robyn Dawes showed in 1979 that simple models, adding up equally weighted factors, can predict outcomes as well as or better than a clinician's holistic judgement.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Models apply the same rule every time, while people vary with mood and fatigue. Even crude scoring cuts that inconsistency. It works best for repeated decisions with known predictors.

Example: A hiring team lists four skills, rates each candidate one to five, and adds the scores. This beats a gut feeling formed in a chatty interview.

Apply it today: For a repeated choice, such as choosing a flat or a hire, pick four criteria, score every option on each, add the totals, then compare with your gut.

source.title: The robust beauty of improper linear models in decision making
source.author: Robyn M. Dawes

ideas.title: The calcium in your bones was made inside stars
ideas.body: The Big Bang made mostly hydrogen and helium. Heavier elements like carbon, oxygen and calcium were forged in stars and scattered when they died. A 1957 paper by Burbidge, Burbidge, Fowler and Hoyle laid out how.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Stars fuse light atoms into heavier ones, releasing energy. Elements up to iron are formed in cores, and heavier ones need extreme events such as supernovae and neutron star collisions. Each generation of stars enriches the gas for the next.

Example: The Sun and planets formed from gas already seeded by earlier stars. The iron in your blood and the oxygen you breathe were built that way. The claim is not poetry: it follows from nuclear physics checked against what we see.

Apply it today: Look up the periodic table colored by origin, and pick three elements in your body to find where each was made.

source.title: Synthesis of the Elements in Stars
source.author: E. Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey R. Burbidge, William A. Fowler and Fred Hoyle

ideas.title: Contempt does the most damage in a relationship
ideas.body: John Gottman's research on couples singles out contempt, such as sarcasm, mockery, eye-rolling and name-calling, as especially corrosive. It tells your partner that you see them as beneath you.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Gottman named four warning behaviours: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling. Contempt was the strongest predictor of breakup in his work. The antidote he suggests is building a culture of appreciation and respect in everyday moments.

Example: A partner says, 'Great job, genius' after a mistake. The words may be light but the sneer lands as contempt. Saying 'That went wrong, and I'm annoyed; can we fix it?' keeps the complaint without the insult.

Apply it today: Notice one sarcastic jab you make this week. Replace it with a plain statement of what you feel and what you need.

source.title: Why Marriages Succeed or Fail
source.author: John M. Gottman and Nan Silver

ideas.title: Abroad, boil it, cook it, peel it or forget it
ideas.body: The CDC's food and water guidance for travelers: eat food that is cooked and served hot, choose sealed bottled or boiled water, and peel fruit yourself. Be wary of ice, salads, and raw items in places with poor sanitation.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Traveler's diarrhea comes mostly from contaminated food and water. Heat kills most germs, and peeling removes surface contamination. Simple rules reduce your exposure.

Example: In a hot market, you pick a freshly fried snack and a sealed bottle of water over a cold salad and iced drink. You stay well.

Apply it today: Visit a travel clinic before your next trip, and pack ORS sachets. For severe symptoms such as blood in stool or high fever, seek medical care. Ask your clinic for hands-on advice.

source.title: Food and Water Safety (Travelers' Health, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)

ideas.title: Many people would rather get a mild shock than sit alone with their thoughts
ideas.body: In a 2014 study, participants spent six to fifteen minutes alone with nothing to do. Many disliked it, and a notable share of them chose to give themselves an electric shock rather than continue.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Without outside input, the mind needs effort to direct itself, and many people find that uncomfortable. The researchers suggest we are more used to external stimulation than we realise. Practice makes quiet time easier.

Example: You wait in a queue and reach for the phone within seconds. Doing nothing for five minutes feels strangely long.

Apply it today: Sit for five minutes with no phone, book or music. Notice what your mind does, and try again tomorrow.

source.title: Just think: The challenges of the disengaged mind
source.author: Timothy D. Wilson et al.

ideas.title: The deadliest air crash led pilots to learn to speak up
ideas.body: In 1977, two jumbo jets collided on a foggy runway on Tenerife, killing 583 people. A captain began takeoff without clear permission, and a junior crew member's doubts were not pressed. The tragedy fed the development of crew resource management.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Crashes often come from communication, not skill alone. Steep status gaps stop people from challenging the boss, and ambiguous phrases are misheard. Crew resource management trains teams to share concerns, use set phrases and confirm instructions.

Example: After Tenerife, aviation standardized radio language, including saying takeoff only in the actual clearance. Flying has become far safer since. Hospitals and other teams have adopted similar checklists and speaking-up routines.

Apply it today: Next time you doubt a decision at work, say it once, plainly, with a question such as: can we check this before we go?

source.title: Tenerife airport disaster

ideas.title: Phone distraction during time together hurts relationship satisfaction
ideas.body: Researchers found that 'phubbing', ignoring a partner in favour of your phone, was linked to more conflict over phone use and lower relationship satisfaction.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: James Roberts and Meredith David surveyed adults in romantic relationships. Partner phubbing was tied to lower satisfaction, partly because it made partners feel ignored. The link is correlational, but the mechanism of lost attention is plausible.

Example: At dinner you glance at your phone between sentences. Your partner stops talking mid-story. Putting phones in another room for the meal ends that dynamic.

Apply it today: Choose one meal or one hour this week as phone-free with someone you care about. Put the phones out of reach before you start.

source.title: My life has become a major distraction from my cell phone: Partner phubbing and relationship satisfaction among romantic partners
source.author: James A. Roberts and Meredith E. David

ideas.title: Know when you last had a tetanus shot before a dirty wound
ideas.body: The CDC recommends a tetanus booster every 10 years. After a deep or dirty wound, such as a puncture from a rusty nail or soil contamination, a booster is advised if it has been 5 years or more since your last dose. Wash the wound and see a doctor.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Tetanus bacteria live in soil and enter through broken skin, and the disease is serious but preventable with vaccination. Wound care and boosters work together.

Example: A gardener spears her hand on a fork in the soil. She cleans it, finds her last shot was seven years ago, and visits an urgent care clinic for a booster.

Apply it today: Find the date of your last tetanus shot in your health records. For a deep wound, bleeding that will not stop, or signs of infection, seek care. Take a hands-on first aid class.

source.title: Tetanus: Wound Management (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)

ideas.title: Trust intuition only where the world is regular and feedback is quick
ideas.body: Kahneman and Klein agreed that expert intuition can be trusted when the environment is stable enough to learn from and the expert has had lots of practice with clear feedback.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Chess players and firefighters learn real patterns. Stock pickers and long-range forecasters work where cues are weak and feedback is slow, so confident intuition there is not evidence of skill. Ask about the environment, not the person's confidence.

Example: A nurse senses a patient is deteriorating before the numbers show it. She has seen that pattern many times. A pundit confidently predicting next year's election has no comparable training signal.

Apply it today: Before relying on a gut feeling, ask two questions: have I seen many similar cases, and did I get quick feedback on them? If either answer is no, check with data.

source.title: Conditions for intuitive expertise: A failure to disagree
source.author: Daniel Kahneman and Gary Klein

ideas.title: Skyscrapers needed a brake that works when the rope breaks
ideas.body: Before 1854, people feared elevators because a cable snap meant a fall. Elisha Otis showed his safety brake at the New York Crystal Palace by cutting the rope while standing on the platform. The brake caught, and building upward became less risky.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: The device is a spring-loaded system that normally stays out of the way. If tension in the rope vanishes, the spring pushes toothed bars into notches in the guide rails and stops the car. Safety comes from a design that fails safe, not from hoping nothing fails.

Example: With safe lifts, upper floors became desirable and tall buildings grew. Modern elevators use multiple cables and speed governors. The idea of a passive safeguard is used in trains, doors and machines.

Apply it today: Look at something you use daily, like a stove or a car, and name the safeguard that works when you do nothing.

source.title: Elevator

ideas.title: Having people to lean on cushions the damage of stress
ideas.body: Sheldon Cohen and Thomas Wills reviewed evidence for the buffering hypothesis: that social support protects people from the harmful effects of stress. Support matters most when stress is high.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Support can change how a stressor is judged, offering reassurance and practical help, and reduce its impact on health. The review found both a general benefit of social ties and a specific buffer for those under pressure.

Example: After a layoff, one person tells friends and gets leads and a place to talk. Another keeps quiet and ruminates alone. The first is likelier to cope well.

Apply it today: When something is weighing on you this week, tell one person you trust. Be specific about whether you want advice or just a listener.

source.title: Stress, social support, and the buffering hypothesis
source.author: Sheldon Cohen and Thomas A. Wills

ideas.title: Switch on government emergency alerts in your phone settings
ideas.body: Wireless Emergency Alerts are short messages sent to phones in a danger area, such as severe weather or missing children. FEMA says you do not need to sign up, but check your phone settings to ensure emergency alerts are on.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Alerts reach you by location, even when networks are busy, and they can come before a storm arrives. They only help if the setting is on and you read and act on them.

Example: A tornado warning alert buzzes a family's phones at night. They wake, go to their basement, and wait out the storm.

Apply it today: Check your phone's notification settings for emergency alerts today. Join a CERT course for hands-on disaster training.

source.title: Wireless Emergency Alerts (FEMA)

ideas.title: Admitting a small flaw can make a capable person more likeable
ideas.body: The pratfall effect: Elliot Aronson found that a highly competent person who made a small blunder, spilling coffee, was rated more likeable than one who did not. For an average person, the blunder lowered ratings.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: A small mistake makes an impressive person seem human and approachable. It only works if competence is already clear. The finding comes from limited studies, so treat it as a tendency.

Example: A senior engineer opens a talk by admitting she once crashed the production server. The room relaxes and listens more.

Apply it today: Where you are already credible, share one small mistake or doubt in your next talk or meeting. Do not fake it.

source.title: The effect of a pratfall on increasing interpersonal attractiveness
source.author: Elliot Aronson, Ben Willerman and Joanne Floyd

ideas.title: Prohibition cut some drinking and created a criminal industry
ideas.body: From 1920 to 1933, the United States banned making and selling alcohol. Reports suggest drinking fell at first. But illegal supply grew through bootleggers and speakeasies, and organized crime profited. The ban was repealed by the Twenty-first Amendment.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Banning something people want does not remove demand. It moves it into black markets, where prices are high, violence settles disputes, and quality is unsafe. Enforcement costs and lost tax revenue also add up. The lesson is about weighing side effects with goals.

Example: Gangs like Al Capone's grew rich on the trade. At the same time, historians note that alcohol-related health harms, such as liver disease, fell during the period. Policies have both benefits and costs worth measuring.

Apply it today: Pick a rule you know of and list one intended effect and one likely side effect. Then ask which evidence would show each.

source.title: Prohibition in the United States

ideas.title: Praise a child's effort, not their intelligence
ideas.body: In studies with fifth graders, children praised for intelligence after a task later chose easier challenges and did worse after failure, compared with children praised for effort.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck found that praising ability made children feel it was fixed and fragile, so they avoided risk. Effort praise showed that progress comes from work, which made hard tasks less threatening.

Example: A child finishes a puzzle. 'You're so smart' makes them worry about the next one. 'You stuck with that even when it got tricky' encourages them to try another.

Apply it today: Next time you praise a child, name something they did, such as a strategy, a try or a choice, and skip the label.

source.title: Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance
source.author: Claudia M. Mueller and Carol S. Dweck

ideas.title: Pay online with a credit card, which gives you stronger dispute rights
ideas.body: The Federal Trade Commission notes that credit cards offer legal protections to dispute charges, while payments by wire transfer, gift card, cryptocurrency or cash app are hard or impossible to reverse. Use a credit card for online buying.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: In the US, the Fair Credit Billing Act lets you dispute billing errors and unauthorized charges on credit cards. Scammers prefer payment methods that cannot be undone.

Example: A shopper pays for a bargain jacket by credit card. The jacket never arrives, so she files a dispute and gets her money back.

Apply it today: Use one credit card for online purchases and check your statements weekly. Report fraud to your bank and the FTC. Join a local consumer protection workshop for hands-on practice.

source.title: Paying for Things (Federal Trade Commission)

ideas.title: Asking for advice makes you look more competent
ideas.body: Brooks, Gino and Schweitzer found that people asked for advice were rated more competent, especially when the task was hard and the request was for advice rather than just an answer.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: People are flattered when asked, and asking shows you care about quality. Most people fear that asking exposes ignorance, but the evidence points the other way when asked of the right person.

Example: A new employee asks a senior colleague how she would approach a difficult client. The colleague later praises her to the manager.

Apply it today: This week, ask someone with relevant experience for advice on a real problem, and ask what they would do in your place.

source.title: Smart people ask for (my) advice: Seeking advice boosts perceptions of competence
source.author: Alison Wood Brooks, Francesca Gino and Maurice E. Schweitzer

ideas.title: Fuel prices swing wildly because people cannot quickly cut how much they buy
ideas.body: Price elasticity of demand measures how much buying changes when price changes. For gasoline in the short run, it is low: people still need to drive to work. So a small shortage can cause a big price jump to squeeze out enough demand.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: If demand barely responds, a small drop in supply needs a large price rise to balance the market. In the long run, people can switch to efficient cars, move closer to work or take transit, so demand is more elastic. Time changes how flexible choices are.

Example: A storm that shuts one refinery can push pump prices up quickly. A tax on a product with inelastic demand raises revenue without changing behavior much. Luxuries with close substitutes behave the opposite way.

Apply it today: Pick three things you buy and rank them by how much you would cut back if prices rose a quarter. That ranking is your own elasticity.

source.title: Price elasticity of demand

ideas.title: Take at least twenty minutes to cool down when an argument floods you
ideas.body: When an argument gets heated, your heart pounds and you stop listening well. John Gottman calls this flooding. His advice is to take a break of at least 20 minutes, do something calming, and come back to the talk.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: A racing body can't think clearly, and fresh arguments from a flooded state tend to go badly. Twenty minutes gives the stress response time to settle. Say when you will come back, so the break doesn't feel like abandonment.

Example: Mid-argument, you say, 'I'm too worked up to talk well. Can we pause for half an hour and then come back?' You walk around the block, then sit down and talk calmly.

Apply it today: Agree with a partner or close person now on a pause phrase to use in a heated moment, and what each of you will do during the break.

source.title: The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work
source.author: John M. Gottman and Nan Silver

ideas.title: Guaranteed returns on an investment mean it is probably a scam
ideas.body: The Federal Trade Commission warns that real investments never guarantee profits. Be suspicious of anyone who pushes you to invest quickly, claims no risk, or sends you to a website to deposit money, especially in crypto.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Scammers show fake dashboards with growing balances to lure bigger deposits, then block withdrawals. Pressure and secrecy are tactics to stop you from checking.

Example: A message offers 'guaranteed' returns through a trading app. The recipient searches the company in the regulator's register, finds nothing, and reports the account.

Apply it today: Before investing, check that the seller is registered with your financial regulator. Talk to a trusted person first. Join a financial scam awareness class for hands-on practice.

source.title: What To Know About Cryptocurrency and Scams (Federal Trade Commission)
